title: Avoiding scams
examples: What are some common types of online scams I should watch out for?
How can I check if a website or email is legitimate?
What should I do if I think I have been targeted by a scam?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to spot potential scams.

items: Requests for secrecy: asking you not to tell anyone
Too good to be true: unbelievable offers

explain.say: A major red flag is unexpected communication about money.
Another warning sign is poor communication quality on a site.
Verification means confirming information through trusted sources.
Always verify the sender's identity through official, known phone numbers.
In real life, if you get a call about a bank issue, hang up first.

faq.q: What is the best way to check if a website is real?
faq.a: Check the website's domain name carefully for misspellings. Also, look for clear contact information and a physical address.
asks: How do I check website legitimacy?
What should I look for on a website?

faq.q: Are emails from companies always safe?
faq.a: No, scammers can easily fake email addresses. Always hover over the sender's email address to see the true source.
asks: How can I tell if an email is fake?
Is email proof of sender identity?

faq.q: If something sounds too good to be true, is it always a scam?
faq.a: It is a very strong indicator of a scam. Legitimate opportunities usually require some level of effort or vetting.
asks: What if an offer is amazing?
Is 'too good to be true' a warning sign?

faq.q: Should I ever give out my passwords over the phone?
faq.a: Never give out passwords or PINs over the phone or email. Legitimate organizations will never ask for this information that way.
asks: Can I trust phone calls for passwords?
Who should I give my password to?

faq.q: What if I already clicked a suspicious link?
faq.a: Do not click anything else on that site. Immediately disconnect your device from the internet and run antivirus software.
asks: What to do after clicking a bad link?
Immediate steps after a potential breach?

facts: Scammers often create a sense of urgency to prevent you from thinking clearly.
Always use official, independently verified contact methods for important services.
If a request involves transferring money quickly, it warrants extra scrutiny.
Professional organizations usually require you to verify credentials through their main website.

quiz.say: A message demanding immediate payment to avoid account closure is likely:
quiz.why: Scammers use urgency to stop you from thinking critically or verifying the claim.

wrong.1: Legitimate warnings usually provide time and clear steps for resolution.
wrong.2: Technical glitches usually have automated, traceable error codes.
wrong.3: Tax notices usually come through formal, mailed channels.

quiz.say: To verify a job offer, you should:

options.show: Use the phone number on the letterhead
options.say: Use the phone number on the letterhead

options.show: Ask a friend to call the number
options.say: Ask a friend to call the number

options.show: Call the company using a number from their official website.
options.say: Call the company using a number from their official website.

quiz.why: This prevents you from calling a number the scammer might have provided.

wrong.0: The scammer may have printed fake letterhead documents.
wrong.1: A friend might not know the correct, current contact number.
wrong.3: The scammer controls the email thread and can mislead you.

quiz.say: Which of these is a strong red flag?

options.show: The email has a strange logo
options.say: The email has a strange logo

options.show: The offer guarantees high returns with no risk.
options.say: The offer guarantees high returns with no risk.

quiz.why: In finance, high returns always come with some level of risk.

wrong.0: A strange logo can sometimes be part of a legitimate rebranding.
wrong.1: Scammers can copy highly formal language to appear credible.
wrong.2: Asking for details is normal when setting up an account.
